articles.title: Flock Employee Calls Cops on Reporter Filming Them
articles.description: Flock Safety wants to record millions of Americans—but apparently no one is allowed to record them. The disturbing double standard was revealed Tuesday by Atlanta News First , which found itself in a load of trouble after one of its investigative reporters stopped on the side of the road to film a Flock Safety employee upgrading one of the company’s cameras near his house. Brendan Keefe—a Peabody-, duPont-, Murrow-, and Emmy-winning journalist—pulled ahead of the Flock Safety site in a marked press van, donned a high-visibility vest, and began snapping pictures. Almost immediately, the Flock Safety employee chucked his equipment into his truck and fled the site. Keefe tried to tail the vehicle, but his efforts were interrupted by the Milton Police Department, who sent out three police vehicles after the Flock employee summoned them. “I work with Flock Safety and I’m getting followed, harassed, pretty much, taking video and pictures,” the employee said in a 9-1-1 call obtained by the local news network. When the operator prompted the employee to provide his name, he opted not to, claiming that he didn’t “want them to hear my full name” on the call “when they get it.” Taking pictures and videos in public spaces, where there is no reasonable expectation of privacy, is protected under the First Amendment. But Flock Safety’s close relationship with police departments across the country seems to have afforded the company protections beyond the scope of the Constitution. “When you are lawfully present in a public space—such as streets, sidewalks, and parks—the First Amendment generally protects your right to photograph or film anything in plain view, including federal buildings and law enforcement,” according to the American Civil Liberties Union . Flock Safety deployed its first mass surveillance camera (which was, at the time, an Android phone placed inside a waterproof box) in Atlanta in 2017. Since then, the company has deployed tens of thousands of cameras to record and document the movements of everyday Americans, regardless of whether or not they’re suspected of a crime. That data is then sold to law enforcement agencies, offering them a seemingly infinite porthole into the potentially consequential habits of their countrymen. In April, the company—and its business model—were valued at $8.4 billion. In most cases, the cameras were installed without community consent. The company has repeatedly defended its product, claiming that the cameras have provided more safety , and that the cited abuses stem from the way that police use their data, rather than the collective of the data itself. “Ultimately, I would argue that the whole community is our customer,” Flock Safety Chief Communications Officer Josh Thomas told Atlanta News First. “Why can’t I opt out? Why can’t the spouse or ex-spouse of a police officer opt out of this kind of data collection on their movements?” asked Keefe. “Why can’t a person opt out?” repeated Thomas. “It’s because if your car gets stolen, if something were to happen, moreover the government requires you to have a license plate.” “It’s plain viewing information,” Thomas continued, missing the bitter irony of the situation. “Why can’t you opt out? You can, if you want to opt out of society.”

articles.title: Sindh Assembly rejects demand for independent commission to probe HIV outbreak
articles.description: • Muttahida MPA’s resolution turned down by treasury benches • Sharjeel slams federal ministers for launching campaign against 18th Amendment • Calls upon Centre to end ‘discrimination’ in gas and electricity supply to Sindh KARACHI: The Sindh Assembly on Monday rejected with majority votes an opposition resolution seeking constitution of an independent commission to probe the HIV/AIDS outbreak in the province. Muttahida Qaumi Movement-Pakistan lawmaker Muhammad Aamir Siddiqui tabled a resolution in the house and expressed serious concern over the HIV outbreak in a Sindh Employees Social Security Institution (SESSI)-run hospitals. According to his resolution: “This House expresses serious concern over the HIV-related issue reported at Valika Hospital and its possible impact on public health. This House recommends that the Government of Sindh constitute an independent commission to investigate the matter and determine whether HIV has spread beyond the reported cases and the extent of the issue across the province. “The House further recommends that, until the completion of the inquiry, the concerned officers responsible for the matter be removed from their posts.” Labour Minister Saeed Ghani opposed the resolution, saying work on the issue was already underway and an endowment fund had been established. He urged the mover to withdraw his resolution. However, Mr Siddiqui preferred his resolution to be placed for a vote in the house, which rejected it with the majority votes of treasury members. It may be noted that a couple of weeks ago the Sindh government had confirmed that over 100 children had been infected with HIV at Valika Hospital. It had set up a Rs2bn endowment fund for treatment and rehabilitation of affected children and their families. Members’ absence irked speaker The proceedings were hampered due to the absence of members, as neither the movers of five resolutions nor the lawmakers who had submitted questions were present in the house. The session, chaired by Speaker Syed Owais Qadir Shah, could not take up most of the items on the agenda. With no mover present, all five resolutions scheduled for submission lapsed. During Question Hour relating to the public health engineering department, no member was present to ask supplementary questions, following which the chair concluded it. Expressing displeasure over the poor attendance, the speaker said that it had become a practice for members to submit questions and resolutions but remain absent when the business was taken up. “The minister has come prepared, but members are absent,” he remarked. The speaker directed that members ensure their presence and stressed that seriousness was required for the effective functioning of the house. The listed questions were submitted by the MQM-P members Muhammad Daniyal and Syed Muhammad Usman, who were not present in the house during Question Hour. In reply to a private motion by MQM-P MPA Quratulain seeking installation of street lights on all highways, Senior Minister Sharjeel Inam Memon said that all national highways fell under the jurisdiction of the federal government. He asked the member to raise the matter with her party’s representatives in the National Assembly. Sharjeel slams federal ministers, defends 18th Amendment Mr Memon then launched a detailed defence of the 18th Amendment, criticising recent statements by federal ministers including Khalid Maqbool Siddiqui, Ahsan Iqbal, Khawaja Asif and Mustafa Kamal. “Provinces have become autonomous after the 18th Amendment,” he said. He accused the federal ministers of launching a regrettable campaign against to raise the matter with her party’s representatives in the National Assembly. Sharjeel slams federal ministers, defends 18th Amendment Mr Memon then launched a detailed defence of the 18th Amendment, criticising recent statements by federal ministers including Khalid Maqbool Siddiqui, Ahsan Iqbal, Khawaja Asif and Mustafa Kamal. “Provinces have become autonomous after the 18th Amendment,” he said. He accused the federal ministers of launching a regrettable campaign against the 18th Amendment and demanded that the federation end what he termed discrimination in gas and electricity supply to the province. The senior minister said that provinces had made significant gains in health, education and energy since the passage of the 18th Amendment, and critics in Islamabad should first review those results instead of questioning provincial autonomy. “If Mustafa Kamal, Ahsan Iqbal, Khawaja Asif or any other federal minister has any objection to the 18th Amendment or the powers of the provinces, then they should come and speak in parliament,” he said, adding: “We have representatives in this assembly who are capable of answering every question constitutionally, legally and with statistics.” Citing the Jinnah Postgraduate Medical Centre and the National Institute of Cardiovascular Diseases as examples, the senior minister said that both institutions had transformed after devolution. “NICVD is considered one of the best medical institutions in Pakistan. Thousands of people from across the country come there for free treatment. This is the result of this system and the powers given to the provinces,” he said. Mr Memon said that more than 3,500 megawatts of electricity was being generated from Thar coal and fed into the national grid. “This electricity is not only for Sindh or any one city, but for the whole of Pakistan,” he said. He further said universities and modern medical facilities had been established in cities like Sukkur, and that the provincial health department was now “standing on its own feet”. The minister said that the residents were bearing the brunt of loadshedding despite the province’s contribution to the national grid. Criticising power utilities for punishing people, he said: “If 20 people have not paid [their bills], take action against those 20. Where is the justice in punishing an entire village?” Mr Memon said collective punishment violated basic constitutional principles. “An entire region cannot be punished because a few people have not paid their bills,” he said. The senior minister also raised the issue of natural gas, saying Sindh had been producing large quantities for years but did not receive its due share. He further questioned the disparity in infrastructure development, noting that Punjab’s motorway network had been built with federal funds. He said that when motorways were built in Punjab, the credit was given to provincial government, although they were federal projects. “Sindh is also a part of this federation, so why is there discrimination against Sindh,” he asked. The senior minister said that to date, a complete motorway network was not built across Sindh comparable to the one in Punjab. Later, the house was adjourned to Tuesday (today). Published in Dawn, September 8th, 2026

articles.title: Ivanka Trump draws scorn with tone-deaf horse-riding video amid economic woes
articles.description: President Donald Trump's eldest daughter is drawing online scorn after posting a video of herself enjoying an oceanside horse ride. On Monday, Ivanka Trump posted the video of her racing a horse on the beach in front of a setting sun and scored it to "Viva la Vida" by Coldplay. Commentators gave more than an online roll of the eyes as they blasted Ivanka for posting the video while her father presides over high gas prices and a troubled economy. In a post on X, political journalist Carla Marinucci described the video as the "2026 version" of Marie Antoinette's "Let them eat cake." "Bro," wrote MeidasTouch political commentator Ben Meiselas. "These people are actually demons." "I need to see this whole family in jail so badly," reacted progressive political commentator Jack Cocchiarella. Media personality and political strategist Keith Edwards noted that Ivanka posted the video and turned off the ability for anyone to reply to it. "Turning off replies," Edwards posted . "She knows." Republican podcaster Melissa Witte juxtaposed the Trump family's messaging by pointing out that Kai Trump posted a video about her luxury dorm that day. "Americans: We can't afford gas, food or tuition," Witte wrote on X. "Trump family: here's a video of Kai's luxury dorm, Ivanka riding a horse and we're also gonna rename both New Mexico and Lake Ontario 'America.'" MAGA journalist Eric Spracklen similarly wrote , "Americans: $4 a gallon gas is killing me," and then "Trumps:" above the video. The official account for the press office of California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) reacted to Ivanka's video by simply writing, "OK," above a screenshot of an article with the headline "Fuel prices at record Labor Day high in US thanks to Iran war and refinery issues." Likewise, Georgia state Rep. Ruwa Romman responded to Ivanka's video by posting a screenshot of a New York Times article headlined, "Under Trump, protected wild horses are going to the slaughter," which is about the Trump administration sending wild horses to be killed and eaten abroad.
